Methodius of Olympus
meh-THOH-dee-us of oh-LIM-pus
proper noun
From the Greek Methōdios, from methōdos, “a following after, a pursuit, a method” (from metá, after, and hodós, way). He is styled “of Olympus” from the Lycian see he is traditionally held to have governed, dying a martyr about 311.

📖 Biblical Definition

Methodius of Olympus was an early bishop and confessor of the church, remembered chiefly as one of the first to contend openly against certain errors of Origen, that learned and influential teacher whose speculations upon the pre-existence of souls and the shape of the resurrection body strayed from the plain testimony of Scripture. Where Origen tended to allegorize away the resurrection of the flesh and to entertain the pre-existence of the soul, Methodius laboured to hold the church to the sober hope of the bodily resurrection, that this same body, sown in corruption, shall be raised in incorruption, 1 Corinthians 15:42, and that the man who dies is the man who shall rise. His best-known work, the Symposium or Banquet of the Ten Virgins, sets forth in the form of a discourse the praise of purity and virginity, drawing upon the parable of the wise and foolish virgins to commend a watchful and holy chastity while awaiting the Bridegroom. Though not every judgment in his writings is to be followed, and though his high estimate of virginity must be weighed against the honour Scripture gives to marriage, his stand for the resurrection of the body against speculative error, and his death as a martyr under Diocletian’s persecution, mark him as a faithful witness whose labour helped to guard the church’s hope.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An early bishop and martyr who opposed the errors of Origen and defended the bodily resurrection, author of the Symposium.

METHODIUS OF OLYMPUS, proper noun. An early Christian bishop, traditionally of Olympus in Lycia, and a martyr about 311.

One of the first to contend openly against the speculative errors of Origen touching pre-existence and the resurrection.

A defender of the resurrection of the flesh, that this same body shall be raised incorruptible.

Author of the Symposium, or Banquet of the Ten Virgins, a discourse in praise of purity drawn from the parable of the virgins.

A confessor who sealed his testimony in martyrdom under the Diocletian persecution.

📖 Key Scripture

1Co 15:42 — "So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:"

Job 19:26 — "And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God:"

Mat 25:1 — "Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom."

Dan 12:3 — "And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness against speculative error, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the church’s hope of the bodily resurrection.

expand to see more

Methodius’s labour was itself a defence of the truth against the errors of his age, for he stood against Origen’s speculations touching the pre-existence of souls and the dissolving of the resurrection body into allegory, holding fast instead to the plain apostolic hope that this same flesh, sown in corruption, shall be raised in incorruption, 1 Corinthians 15:42.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover through his life is the sober, literal hope of the resurrection of the body, which the church confesses against every philosophy that would spiritualize it away, and the watchfulness of the wise virgins who keep their lamps trimmed against the coming of the Bridegroom. That a man of the early church saw clearly enough to correct so towering a teacher as Origen reminds us that faithfulness to Scripture, not the reputation of a name, is the measure of truth, and that the resurrection of the flesh is no myth but the settled promise of God.

That the same body which dies shall be raised, and that faithfulness corrects even the most celebrated teacher.

Usage
